s: If this type comes, solve like this

s.q: If it gives $\alpha^n+\beta^n$ (or $P_n$, $S_n$, $a_n$) and asks for a ratio/combination of high powers
s.n: 1) Write the recurrence from the equation. 2) Rewrite the asked expression so it becomes $aS_{n+2}+bS_{n+1}$ etc. 3) It collapses to a multiple of one $S_k$. For $\alpha^n-\beta^n$ the same recurrence holds.
s.h: Trap: don't expand powers; with given $P_{10},P_9,P_8$ you can read off $a,b,c$ directly.

s.q: If it asks for a new quadratic whose roots are a function of $\alpha,\beta$
s.f: x^2-(\text{sum of new roots})x+(\text{product of new roots})=0
s.n: 1) Get $\alpha+\beta$, $\alpha\beta$. 2) Express the new sum and product symmetrically. 3) For simple maps ($\frac1\alpha$, $k\alpha$, $\alpha+k$) just substitute $x\to\frac1x$, $\frac xk$, $x-k$ in the original.

s.q: If roots must lie in an interval, on one side of $k$, or both be positive
s.n: Draw the parabola. Write three conditions: discriminant, sign of $af$ at the end points, position of the vertex. Exactly one root in $(p,q)$: $f(p)f(q)<0$. Intersect all conditions.
s.h: Trap: leading coefficient may be negative or zero — check $a=0$ separately.

s.q: If two quadratics share a root
s.n: Fastest route in JEE: subtract the equations to kill $x^2$ and get the common root $\alpha$ linearly, substitute back. Then use Vieta in each equation for the other roots.

s.q: If the equation is in $e^x$, $a^x$, $(\sqrt3+\sqrt2)^x$ or $\tan^2x$ etc.
s.n: 1) Substitute $t$. 2) Solve the polynomial in $t$ (reciprocal equations: divide by $t^2$, put $u=t+\frac1t$). 3) Keep only $t$ in the allowed range ($t>0$). Count $x$ values.
s.h: Trap: each valid $t$ gives one $x$ for $e^x$, but two for $x^2-4$ inside the exponent.

s.q: If it says "always positive / negative for all $x$" or "real roots" with a parameter
s.n: Write the conditions on the parameter, solve the inequalities, count integers if asked. For "equal roots", set $D=0$; note $x=1$ is often a root of $a(b-c)x^2+\cdots$ so roots are $1$ and $\frac{c}{a}\cdot\ldots$

s.q: If it asks for the range of $\frac{a_1x^2+b_1x+c_1}{a_2x^2+b_2x+c_2}$
s.n: Treat $y$ as a parameter, require real $x$, solve the inequality in $y$; exclude $y$ values that come only from excluded $x$.

s.q: If roots must be integers / rational
s.f: D\ \text{is a perfect square};\ \ \text{irrational roots come in conjugate pairs}
s.n: For $x^2+4x-n=0$: $D=16+4n$ must be a perfect square → list $n$. For integer-root pairs use $\alpha+\beta$, $\alpha\beta$ factor pairs.

s.q: If the question is a cubic/symmetric value like $a^4+b^4+c^4$ from $\sum a$, $\sum ab$, $abc$
If it is a log / surd / modulus equation that becomes quadratic
s.n: Factor arguments (e.g. $2x^2+7x+5=(x+1)(2x+5)$), use $\log_ab\cdot\log_ba=1$ to get $t+\frac2t$ forms; then check domain (base $>0$, $\ne1$).

s.q: If it is a continued fraction $a+\frac1{b+\frac1{a+\cdots}}$
Odd-ones (polynomial with shifted terms, functional root conditions)
s.f: \text{expand sums with } \sum k,\ \sum k^2;\ \ \alpha\mapsto\alpha^2-2\ \text{map: test fixed points and 2-cycles}
s.n: For "whenever $\alpha$ is a root so is $\alpha^2-2$": roots are fixed points of $x^2-2=x$ or a 2-cycle; list the pairs.
